notes: Haggai is a short, tightly-dated book (2 chapters, 38 verses; all four messages fall within about four months of Darius I's 2nd regnal year). Only two named human figures beyond the prophet himself appear: Zerubbabel (governor) and Joshua son of Josedech (high priest), always addressed together. No submanagers were warranted — the "remnant of the people" acts only as an undifferentiated group and is cited within the entries their actions belong to, not given a separate entry. Two law/theme tiers were split out because they are each independently load-bearing: the temple-rebuilding charge (the book's central theme, 1:2-11/2:1-9) and the priests' ceremonial-defilement ruling (2:10-19), which is a distinct, self-contained teaching rather than a restatement of the temple charge. Darius is included as a standalone "named" entry (dating anchor only, appears in every date formula) rather than folded silently into other entries, since he is load-bearing for the book's structure but never acts. CORRECTION FROM PRIOR DRAFT: the earlier version's Zerubbabel funFact wrongly claimed Matthew 1:12 and Luke 3:27 disagree on his father's name — they do not; both agree it was Shealtiel/Salathiel. The real, genuine divergence is between those NT genealogies (plus Ezra/Nehemiah/Haggai itself, all naming Shealtiel) and 1 Chronicles 3:19, which instead names Zerubbabel's father as Pedaiah, Shealtiel's brother — one generation off from what the prior draft claimed. This has been corrected in Zerubbabel's genealogy.note and removed from funFacts to avoid duplication/drift.

characters.name: Haggai the prophet
characters.perkNote: Every one of his four messages carries an exact date (1:1; 1:15; 2:1; 2:10; 2:20) — the most precisely dated prophetic book in the Minor Prophets.

genealogy.note: No genealogy is given for Haggai anywhere in scripture — not even a tribal or family background is stated, unlike his contemporary Zechariah ("son of Berechiah, son of Iddo," Zechariah 1:1).

verses.note: Dated to Darius's 2nd year, 6th month, day 1 — the LORD's word comes "by Haggai the prophet" to Zerubbabel and Joshua.
Rebukes the people for living in "cieled houses" while the LORD's house "lieth waste"; ties recent crop failure/drought directly to this neglect.
Called "the LORD's messenger" delivering the LORD's own reassurance, "I am with you."
Second message: encourages the discouraged builders, promises "the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former."
Cross-reference outside this book: named alongside Zechariah the son of Iddo as one of the two prophets who prophesied to spur the temple rebuilding under Darius.
Cross-reference: the elders of the Jews build successfully "through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo."

funFacts: Tenth of the twelve Minor Prophets in canonical order, immediately before Zechariah.
His book covers only about four months of activity, entirely within Darius I's second regnal year (c. 520 BC).
He is the only prophet in the book explicitly given the title "the LORD's messenger" (1:13) rather than the more common "thus saith the LORD" formula alone.

characters.name: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel
characters.perkNote: Singled out alone (without Joshua) in the book's final oracle and named "my servant" and a "signet" of the LORD — his line carries messianic weight into Matthew and Luke's genealogies of Jesus.

genealogy.note: Called "the son of Shealtiel" throughout Haggai (1:1, 1:12, 1:14, 2:2, 2:23), matching Ezra 3:2, Nehemiah 12:1, and the NT genealogies at Matthew 1:12 and Luke 3:27 (Greek form "Salathiel") — all of these agree the father was Shealtiel/Salathiel. The genuine divergence lies elsewhere: 1 Chronicles 3:19 instead lists Zerubbabel as son of Pedaiah, Shealtiel's brother, one generation off from what Haggai/Ezra/Matthew/Luke state — possibly reflecting a levirate-marriage arrangement in which Pedaiah raised up an heir for a childless Shealtiel. This is a real, documented cross-book tension, not a disagreement between the two NT genealogies on the father's name itself.

verses.note: Addressed as "governor of Judah" alongside Joshua the high priest — the book's civil-authority addressee.
Obeys the voice of the LORD along with Joshua and the remnant of the people.
The LORD "stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel" to begin work on the temple.
Told directly, "be strong, O Zerubbabel... and work: for I am with you."
Final oracle addressed to him alone ("the second time... unto Zerubbabel"): promised he will be made "as a signet," chosen by the LORD amid the shaking of kingdoms.

funFacts: His title "governor of Judah" (pechah) reflects a Persian-appointed provincial administrator, not a king — Judah had no throne at this time.

The 2:23 signet promise directly reverses Jeremiah 22:24, where the LORD says He would pluck Zerubbabel's grandfather Coniah/Jehoiachin off "though he were the signet upon my right hand" — Haggai restores that very signet imagery to Coniah's line.
Appears in both Matthew 1:12-13 and Luke 3:27 as an ancestor of Jesus, though the two genealogies list different sons of his beyond that point.

characters.name: Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest
characters.perkNote: The addressee, alongside the priests, of the book's ceremonial-law question in 2:11-13 — his office is what makes that ruling authoritative.

genealogy.note: KJV spells his father's name "Josedech" here and in Zechariah (3:1, 6:11), but "Jehozadak" in Ezra (3:2, 3:8, 10:18), Nehemiah 12:26, and 1 Chronicles 6:14-15 — same person, a deliberate KJV spelling difference across books, not normalized here. Naming collision flag: this Joshua is a different person from Joshua son of Nun, Moses' successor who led Israel into Canaan generations earlier — no relation, name only.

verses.note: Addressed as "the high priest" alongside Zerubbabel — the book's religious-authority addressee.
Obeys the voice of the LORD along with Zerubbabel and the remnant of the people.
The LORD "stirred up... the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest" to begin the temple work.
Told directly, "be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest... and work: for I am with you."
Present as the priestly-office holder when Haggai poses the LORD's question about holiness/defilement to "the priests."

funFacts: Paired with Zerubbabel as joint addressee of every message in the book — civil and religious leadership approached together throughout.
Also called "Jeshua" (a KJV spelling variant of the same name) in Ezra and Nehemiah, e.g. Ezra 3:2 "Jeshua the son of Jozadak."

characters.name: The Rebuilding of the House of the LORD
characters.perkNote: The book's central charge: stop building your own paneled houses and finish the LORD's house first — production only truly begins once the foundation work resumes (2:18-19).
characters.purpose: To reorder the returned exiles' priorities after they had let the temple's reconstruction stall for years while finishing their own houses (1:2-4, 1:9). Ties recent crop failure and economic futility directly to this neglect (1:6, 1:10-11), then, once work resumes, promises the rebuilt "latter house" will exceed the former Solomonic temple's glory (2:9) and that from the very day the foundation is (re-)laid, the LORD will bless (2:18-19). (Attribution: Haggai the prophet, by the word of the LORD)

verses.note: The people say "the time is not come" to build, while living in their own paneled houses — the charge that opens the book.
Poor harvests and drought explained as consequence of the house lying waste while everyone runs to his own house.
Work actually begins on the 24th day of the 6th month.
Compares the modest new foundation to Solomon's temple, but promises greater latter glory, ending "in this place will I give peace."
Marks the day the temple's foundation was laid as the turning point for blessing: "from this day will I bless you."

funFacts: This second temple's foundation had actually been laid years earlier under Cyrus (Ezra 3:8-10) but construction stalled amid local opposition (Ezra 4) — Haggai's charge is to resume, not to start from nothing.
The finished second temple (later renovated by Herod) is the temple standing in Jesus' day in the Gospels.

characters.name: The Priests' Ruling on Holiness and Defilement
characters.perkNote: A two-question ceremonial-law ruling used to argue that the nation's uncleanness (not holiness) was the thing spreading to their offerings and work.
characters.purpose: At the LORD's instruction, Haggai poses two questions to the priests: whether holy meat carried in the fold of a garment sanctifies bread, pottage, wine, oil, or other food it touches (answered no), and whether a person made unclean by touching a dead body defiles those same things by touching them (answered yes, 2:12-13). The point applied: "so is this people... and so is every work of their hands... that which they offer there is unclean" (2:14) — holiness does not spread by mere contact, but uncleanness does, explaining the nation's fruitless labor before the temple work resumed, and setting up the promised blessing "from this day forward." (Attribution: the priests, ruling in answer to a question Haggai posed at the LORD's command)

verses.note: The LORD instructs Haggai to "ask now the priests concerning the law" — the two hypothetical questions and the priests' answers.
Application: "so is this people, and so is this nation before me... and that which they offer there is unclean."
Recalls the earlier crop failures ("smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail") as consequence, before the temple work resumed.
Marks the same day (the 24th of the 9th month) as the turning point: "from this day will I bless you."

funFacts: This is a rare instance in the prophetic books of a prophet formally consulting priests for a technical ruling under the Levitical purity law before delivering his own application of it.

characters.name: Darius the king

verses.note: "In the second year of Darius the king" — opens the book's dating formula; no further description given.
"In the second year of Darius the king" — repeated to date the start of the temple work.
"In the second year of Darius" — dates the priests'-ruling message.

funFacts: Conventionally identified as Darius I of Persia (Darius Hystaspes, reigned c. 522-486 BC), though Haggai itself gives no identifying detail beyond "Darius the king" — the identification comes from the book's historical setting, not its text.

Naming collision flag: at least two other kings named Darius appear elsewhere in scripture — "Darius the Mede" (Daniel 5:31, 6:1) and "Darius the Persian" (Nehemiah 12:22) — conventionally read as different rulers from the Darius dating Haggai, Ezra, and Zechariah, though none of these books draw the distinction explicitly themselves.
